items.stemHtml:
A 27-year-old woman at 9 weeks' gestation has had 3 weeks of persistent nausea and vomiting; she has lost 4% of her body weight. She has no history of thyroid disease and no neck pain. Pulse is 104/min and blood pressure 108/66 mmHg. There is no goiter, eye change or tremor. Laboratory studies:

TestResult
TSH0.05 µU/mL
Free thyroxine (T4)2.1 ng/dL
Total T3Upper limit of normal for pregnancy
TSH-receptor antibodiesNegative
Urine ketones2+

Which of the following is the most appropriate management of her thyroid findings?

options.label: B
options.html: Propylthiouracil until the time of delivery

options.label: C
options.html: Radioactive iodine uptake scan to find the cause

options.label: D
options.html: Supportive care and repeat thyroid tests later

items.explanationHtml:
In the first trimester hCG stimulates the TSH receptor. With hyperemesis, very high hCG can cause gestational transient thyrotoxicosis: low TSH and modestly raised free T4, with T3 rising less, no goiter or eye signs and negative TSH-receptor antibodies. It resolves as hCG falls after about 14–18 weeks. Antithyroid drugs are not indicated; treat the vomiting and dehydration and recheck thyroid tests, using a beta blocker only briefly for troublesome symptoms.

Takeaway: first-trimester hyperthyroxinemia with hyperemesis and negative TSH-receptor antibodies is hCG-driven and needs supportive care, not antithyroid drugs.

whyNot.A: Methimazole is teratogenic in early pregnancy and is not needed for an hCG-mediated, self-limited process.
whyNot.B: Propylthiouracil is the first-trimester choice only for true Graves hyperthyroidism, which negative antibodies and no goiter make unlikely; it also carries a risk of liver injury.
whyNot.C: Radioiodine studies are contraindicated in pregnancy.
whyNot.E: Surgery is reserved for Graves disease that cannot be controlled with drugs.

items.objective: Recognise gestational transient thyrotoxicosis and avoid antithyroid drugs.
